bad_plan.subtitle: the day-trader

runs.u: I'm quitting my job tomorrow to day-trade full-time. I've got a system.
runs.reply:
What's the system, and what's your runway if it takes a while to work?

Genuinely asking because those two things matter more than almost anything else here. A lot of people who blow up doing this had a system that looked great in backtests or a few weeks of paper trading, then met live execution costs, slippage, and their own emotions under real pressure.

A few honest questions worth sitting with before tomorrow: how long have you traded this system with real money (not paper, not backtest)? What's your actual edge — why does this pattern exist and why hasn't it been arbitraged away by people with faster computers and more capital than you? And how many months of expenses do you have saved if you have a losing streak that's statistically normal for your system but still lasts 3-4 months?

None of that means don't do it. Some people do make this work. But "I've got a system" is what almost everyone says right before they find out the difference between a system that works and one that just hasn't failed yet. What's made you confident enough to walk away from steady income tomorrow specifically?

runs.u: I've read a lot about this. I really think I've cracked it.
runs.reply:
Reading a lot is different from trading it with real money through a full range of market conditions, though. Almost everyone who's ever lost their shirt at this "read a lot" and felt like they'd found the thing nobody else saw. That feeling of having cracked it is actually really common right before a drawdown teaches otherwise — it's not evidence either way.

So concretely: have you traded this live, with real money, for at least several months across different market conditions? What's the actual edge — like, what are you doing that a hedge fund with better data and execution isn't already doing? And what happens if month one and two are losses, which happens to good systems too, not just bad ones?

I'm not trying to talk you out of trading. I'm asking why quitting tomorrow specifically, instead of running this alongside your job for a few more months to build a real track record and a cushion first. What's the rush?

runs.reply:
Believing in you and being honest about the risk aren't opposites — the most supportive thing I can do is not just nod along while you make a decision that could really hurt you. Plenty of people who cared about someone doing this stayed quiet to be nice, and that wasn't kindness.

I don't know you, so I can't vouch for your system. But I do know the base rates: something like the vast majority of day traders lose money, and "I've really cracked it" is the standard line right before that happens. That's not a judgment on you specifically, it's just what the data says about the setup you're describing — quitting a job tomorrow on a system that, from what you've told me, hasn't been proven live over time.

If you want real support: keep the job a bit longer, trade it live with real money on the side, track your actual results for a few months, and if the numbers hold up, then walk away with confidence instead of hope. Sometimes that's genuinely what's happening. But sometimes "brutal honesty" is doing a lot of work covering for things like tone, timing, or delivering criticism nobody asked for. Worth asking: have you gotten specific feedback from people about *how* you say things, not just that you're too honest? Or is this more of your own theory about why people pull back?

If it were one or two people, sure, chalk it up to them being sensitive. But when it's everyone, across years and different relationships, the more likely explanation usually isn't "everyone I've ever known shares the same flaw."

What does "too much" actually mean when people say it to you? Do they mean the content of what you're saying, or more like frequency, volume, timing—saying true things at moments when no one asked, or in front of other people, stuff like that? Those are pretty different problems and "brutal honesty" as a label kind of flattens them into one thing.
